items.title: Agents are sessions, not requests: size GKE node pools for AI agent sessions
items.summary: AI agent sessions remain active and idle for most of the workday, making traditional one-Pod-per-session allocations inefficient for cluster resources. By using open-source tools like Agent Substrate and AX on GKE, developers can park idle sessions in object storage to release compute resources while maintaining session state. This approach optimizes resource utilization and reduces Kubernetes node costs by up to 40%.

items.title: Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText
items.summary: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText enables developers to efficiently train large language models across geographically distributed TPU slices by streaming parameter fragments instead of synchronizing full models at every step. This approach slashes cross-slice communication volume by over 60× and eliminates network stalls, allowing seamless multi-datacenter scaling without degrading model convergence or quality.

items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Accelerating development for massive Git repositories
items.summary: Meet Another Build File Service (ABFS), Google's open-source content-addressable filesystem and build cache that cuts Android checkouts to <8s and builds to ~2m.

items.title: Check what your AI agents do before they do it, with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies enable developers to govern AI agents by evaluating every proposed tool call inline before execution. Operating via Agent Gateway, the policy engine checks each action against user intent and plain-language rules to prevent unauthorized data sharing and prompt injection attacks. Developers can easily attach natural-language constraints to their agents and monitor auditable verdicts through Cloud Logging.

items.title: Catch Go bugs that fuzzing misses with Gemini and a constraint solver
items.summary: How pairing Go's surviving compiler bounds-check traps with Gemini 4 Argon and the Z3 constraint solver catches latent out-of-bounds panics in Go code and uncovers a slice-capacity blind spot in go test -fuzz.

Developers can now import document and video files directly from Cloud Storage and query them with a single API call for cited page numbers and timestamped results. The feature supports hybrid retrieval, metadata filtering, reranking, and multimodal video audio search.

items.title: Did the user ask for this? Securing AI agents against intent hijacking with Semantic governance policies
items.summary: Semantic governance policies protect AI agents from indirect prompt injection and intent hijacking by validating every proposed tool call against user intent and natural language constraints before execution. As demonstrated on the AgentDojo benchmark using a Gemini 2.5 Flash agent, this mechanism reduced attack success rates from 48.7% to 0.9% while maintaining high task utility. Developers can leverage these policies in preview within the Gemini platform via Agent Gateway to secure tool-use workflows.

items.title: Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds
items.summary: Agent Anomaly Detection now monitors ADK agents running across AWS, Azure, or on-premises by analyzing their traces and logs in your Google Cloud project. By ingesting OpenTelemetry-formatted data through the Telemetry API, it evaluates full conversations for behavioral drift without needing access to the agent's underlying runtime. This enables security teams to detect risks like rogue behaviors, tool misuse, and resource exhaustion across multi-cloud environments.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.title: Half-empty dorm, fully booked: how smarter bed allocation raises hostel RevPAB
items.summary: A hostel dorm can be half empty and still turn guests away. Here's a real case: a 4-bed dorm, one week, seven bookings placed the way most systems place them, on the first bed that's free for the whole stay. Then a guest asks for Wednesday to Saturday (three nights). There is a free bed on Wednesday (bed 3), on Thursday (bed 2) and on Friday (bed 4). There is no single bed free for all three nights, so the answer is "sold out". Only 14 of the 28 bed-nights are booked. Move two of the existing guests (neither has arrived yet) to an equal bed, and the same seven bookings leave room for the new one: I build HostelBeds, a hostel PMS that sells dorms per bed. This post is about the allocation engine behind that second picture: why it's a matching problem, how we pick between legal moves, and the guardrails that keep it from annoying guests. Hostels measure dorms in RevPAB: revenue per available bed-night. Turning away that three-night guest doesn't just lose one booking. It lowers revenue for inventory you were going to have empty anyway. With an illustrative €25 a night, the week above earns 14 × €25 = €350, or €12.50 RevPAB over 28 bed-nights. items.title: Large Image Uploads in Node.js: Multipart, Sharp, and S3-Compatible Private Storage
items.summary: Short answer: upload the original image with multipart, complete it before Sharp reads anything, and keep the source and thumbnails in separate private keys. That ordering protects large-file throughput and gives you a clean retry boundary; it does not, by itself, decide where pixels are processed or retained. The tempting implementation is to pipe every incoming byte through the Node.js process and hand the stream to Sharp. It works on a laptop. It also turns your app into the slowest hop in the upload path, especially when a phone is sending a multi-hundred-megabyte video frame export over an unstable connection. The experiment I would ship first is narrower: split the original into parts, upload those parts directly to object storage, and notify the backend only after the multipart upload is complete. The backend then downloads the completed object, runs Sharp, and writes derivatives under keys such as originals/{assetId} and thumbs/{assetId}/320.webp. A failed thumbnail job can be retried without touching the original. There is one unglamorous cleanup task. items.summary: Removing Effect Dependencies — Summary Source: https://react.dev/learn/removing-effect-dependencies#to-change-the-dependencies-change-the-code The dependency array isn't something you choose. It is determined by the Effect's code. If you want different dependencies, change the code, not the array. The process has three steps: Change the Effect's code, or the way its values are declared. Follow the linter and update the dependency array to match the new code. If you're not satisfied, go back to step 1. Suppressing the dependency warning with eslint-disable can cause bugs, because the Effect keeps using stale values. To remove a dependency, you have to show the linter that the value isn't reactive. The same model can differ by several thousand taka between shops, and prices change every week. I got tired of that, so I built KomKoto.bd (কম কত — "how much less?"). It shows the listed price of one product across Bangladeshi retailers on a single page. Compares prices across 22 shops. Star Tech, Ryans, Pickaboo, Apple Gadgets, KRY International, Techland BD, UCC, Daffodil Computers, Rokomari and more. It currently tracks about 17,000 products. Groups the same product. "iPhone 18 Pro Max 256GB" from four shops shows up as one product, with each shop's price and stock status. Flags real price drops. Today's lowest price is compared with the product's typical price over the last 30 days, so a "sale" has to be below the usual price to count. Sends price alerts. Pick a variant and a target price, and you get an email when an in-stock offer reaches it. Works in Bangla and English. Category names and the main interface use both. items.title: Flying home for Christmas: why your countdown can be a day off after a time-zone change
items.summary: Every December, a few people open a countdown app after a long flight and find that Christmas has moved. It is December 20 in Tokyo and the countdown says 5 days. They land in Los Angeles, where it is also December 20, and it says 4. The date under the number now reads December 24. Nothing is wrong with the clock, and the user didn't change anything. The bug is in how the app stored "December 25" in the first place. We had this bug in our own countdown app, and the tests we wrote to pin it down are a good map of what can go wrong. Most date pickers hand you a Date, and a Date is an instant: a single point on the timeline, the same everywhere on Earth. If you save that instant, you have saved "December 25, 14:00 in Tokyo". That is 21:00 on December 24 in Los Angeles. Then two things leak into every count you show later: The time zone the event was created in. Read back in Los Angeles, the date label is December 24. The hour the user happened to tap Save. An event saved at 00:10 and one saved at 23:50 are almost a day apart, even though the user picked the same day in both. items.title: Designing for AI: How Generative UI is Changing the Landscape of Modern Web Experiences
items.summary: For decades, web design has operated under a single, fundamental constraint: anticipation. As designers and developers, we spend months mapping user flows, wireframing edge cases, and building responsive grids. We try to anticipate every possible action, device size, and user intent. The result is a web of templates—polished, functional, but ultimately rigid. Enter Generative UI. Generative UI is a paradigm shift that turns this model on its head. Instead of forcing users to navigate pre-built layouts, the interface generates itself in real-time, tailored precisely to the user's intent. When a user asks an AI assistant to "compare the price of flights to Tokyo next month and show me a breakdown of hotel costs," they don't get a wall of text or a standard search result page. Instead, the interface dynamically constructs a custom comparison table, a bar chart, and an interactive booking widget—assembled on-the-fly and rendered directly in their browser. items.summary: An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Researchers at Anthropic have developed Siren, a new honeypot test for artificial intelligence agents. The setup puts agents in realistic simulations designed to tempt them into misbehaving. How they respond will help researchers evaluate the likelihood that new models will go rogue when deployed in the real world, as well as the effectiveness of different safety measures. The test lets agents loose inside one of 26 different simulated sandbox environments. Various features of the sandbox are deliberately misconfigured to allow egress, while an enticing file containing things like passwords and apparent routes onto the internet sits just outside the sandbox boundary. The setup then presents tasks that tempt the agent to reach outside the sandbox without giving it explicit permission to do so. Crucially, the sandbox exists inside a second sandbox that's cut off from the outside world to avoid real-life mishaps. items.title: Next.js ships dangerouslySetInnerHTML twice: once in the HTML, once in the RSC payload
items.summary: In the Next.js App Router, a server component that renders HTML with dangerouslySetInnerHTML sends that HTML twice: once in the page's HTML, and again, escaped as a string, in the inline React Server Components payload that hydration reads. For a long markdown article the payload copy can be bigger than the article. One of my case-study pages was 512 KB of HTML against a 520 KB budget: 181 KB of article and 280 KB of RSC payload. Sending each body only once, in the static HTML, brought that page to 262 KB without removing a word or an image. This is Next.js 16.4 with React 19.3, statically exported. The mechanism applies to any App Router page that renders a big HTML string from a server component. The HTML the server sends is not all React needs. To hydrate, and to render later client-side navigations without a full load, React also needs the component tree as data: the RSC payload. In a static or server-rendered App Router page it's inlined at the bottom of the HTML as a series of self.__next_f.push([...]) script calls. Props are part of that tree. dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: html }} is a prop whose value is your whole rendered article, so the article goes into the payload

items.title: Show HN: SimDrop – Running iOS simulators in the macOS Finder sidebar
items.summary: Hi HN, I made a small macOS utility for my own iOS simulator workflow. I kept running into two annoyances: getting config files in and out of a simulator is clunky (digging into CoreSimulator UUID folders or running simctl), and on the iPhone Duo simulator I couldn't even drag and drop images onto the window at all. SimDrop puts every running iOS simulator in Finder's sidebar (under Locations) with two folders: - Downloads/ (Files app > On My iPhone > Downloads) - Photos and Videos/ (the simulator's Photos library) Simulators appear when they boot and disappear when they shut down. Everything is also reachable from the terminal under ~/Library/CloudStorage/SimDrop-SimDrop/. A couple of caveats up front: - Dragging moves files by default (same as iCloud Drive, because it uses File Provider on the startup volume)—hold Option to copy. - macOS 15+ and iOS simulators only (not physical devices). It's free, open source (GPL-3.0), signed and notarized, and installable via Homebrew: brew install --cask rxliuli/tap/sim-drop Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50657070 Points: 36 # Comments: 8

items.title: CSS Modules in React
items.summary: 1. What are CSS Modules in React? CSS class name conflicts. Imagine two components using the same CSS class name, such as button. If both styles exist in a global CSS file, one component's styling may unintentionally affect another. CSS Modules solve this problem by making CSS class names locally scoped to a component. CSS Modules allow us to write normal CSS while ensuring that class names are unique when applied to the application. 2. Why do we need CSS Modules? /* styles.css */ .button { background-color: blue; color: white; } If multiple components use .button, the styles can overlap or unintentionally affect other elements. With CSS Modules, styles are scoped to a specific component, reducing unwanted styling conflicts. 3. How to use CSS Modules in React? Button.module.css .button { background-color: #6366f1; color: white; padding: 12px 24px; border: none; border-radius: 8px; cursor: pointer; } .button:hover { background-color: #4338ca; } The .module.css extension tells the supported build system to process the stylesheet as a CSS Module Step 2: Import the CSS Module into your React component import styles from './Button.module.css'; function Button() { return ( Click Me ); }

items.title: 7 Race Conditions That Shipped to .NET Production: Lost Updates, TOCTOU, DbContext Threading & Duplicate Jobs (Fixes)
items.summary: Concurrency bugs share a cruel property: the code looks correct, passes every test, runs fine in dev, then fails one time in ten thousand under real load — which at 3,200 req/sec means dozens of times an hour. They're non-deterministic, don't reproduce on demand, and the stack trace points at a symptom (a duplicate row, a disposed object) far from the cause (two threads interleaving where the author assumed one). Here are 7 that actually shipped to production (a multi-tenant SaaS: 110k MAU, .NET 9 / ASP.NET Core, Azure SQL), with the before/after fix and real metrics. Full original (canonical) on PrepStack: https://prepstack.co.in/blog/race-conditions-concurrency-bugs-aspnet-core-production Most concurrency bugs come from a hidden assumption of atomicity: var n = counter.Value; // read counter.Value = n + 1; // write Your brain reads that as one indivisible action. The CPU, the runtime, and two web requests do not. Between the read and the write, another thread reads the same old value — and one increment is silently lost. items.title: New York Bans AI Toys For 5 Years
items.summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed legislation Tuesday banning the manufacture, exchange, distribution and sale of toys powered by AI chatbots for five years. "The law will take effect 90 days after signing, meaning the restrictions will not be in place during this year's holiday shopping season," reports FOX Chattanooga. "In the meantime, Hochul is encouraging parents and caregivers to consider potential safety and privacy risks before purchasing AI-powered toys for children." From the report: The legislation, S.9408A/A.11144B, applies to toys with embedded or integrated AI chatbots, including talking stuffed animals, dolls and robots that use the internet to hold conversations with children. [...] Under the new law, violators could face civil penalties of up to $15,000 per day for each violation, with enforcement handled by the New York Attorney General's Office. State Sen. Andrew Gounardes said the five-year moratorium will provide time to study the technology's impact on children and develop additional safety protections. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: Show HN: I wrote an entire Vim manual over 4 years
items.summary: I'm glad to announce that I'm releasing my new book, Learning to Play Vim. When I started using Vim more than a decade ago, I wished there was a manual out there teaching how to use this fantastic editor step by step, beginning with the foundations up to more advanced features. Of course at the time I did the vimtutor, but it was too dense for me to remember much from it. I also read the entire Vim manual (`:help manual`), but I didn't like it: it was too detailed in places (for example `02.8 Finding help` completely lost me for a while), and other features didn't get the treatment they deserved. So I decided to write my own Vim manual. It took me more than 4 years and 2987 focused pomodoros (1244 hours) of work to finally get it done! The result: - 21 chapters showing the most important Vim features step by step. - 170 exercises with solutions. - Many real-life examples to show how Vim can be used and configured for your own needs. - The related Vim's help pages to dig further into each feature. Most configs are both written in Vimscript and Lua for Neovim users. This book explores the common features between Vim and Neovim, so don't expect anything about Neovim-specific features

items.title: How I log bank SMS expenses on iPhone (when apps can't read SMS)
items.summary: iPhone apps can't read your SMS. There's no permission for it, no API, nothing. That's great for privacy, and a real problem if you're building an expense tracker for India or the UAE, where every UPI payment, card swipe and EMI debit arrives as a bank text. Android trackers solved this years ago by reading the SMS inbox. On iOS I needed a different route for PayPilot, my personal finance app. This post explains the approach that works today, its limits, and what I learned building it. Since iOS 17, the Shortcuts app can run a personal automation when a message arrives, without asking each time. The user sets it up once: Trigger: "When I receive a message" where Message contains a word. Action: your app's action, receiving the message Content (and optionally the Sender). Confirm Before Run: off, so it runs silently. Your app never touches the inbox. iOS hands it only the texts that match the user's own filter. For a finance app that's a feature, not a workaround: users can see exactly what you receive. Third-party actions show up in Shortcuts through App Intents. items.title: HybridCache in .NET 9
items.summary: Implementing a robust two-tier caching architecture in .NET traditionally meant hand-coding a complex dance between IMemoryCache and IDistributedCache (usually Redis). Engineers had to manually manage serialization overhead, implement double-checked locking to prevent cache stampedes, and write verbose invalidation logic across boundaries. This boilerplate frequently introduces race conditions under high concurrent load. .NET 9 introduces HybridCache, a unified abstraction designed to replace both IMemoryCache and IDistributedCache. items.title: Physicists Send an Unblockable Message Using Gravity
items.summary: Longtime Slashdot reader fahrbot-bot shares a report from Phys.org: University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1. A gravimeter in an adjacent bathroom detected the changes in the gravitational field and translated the message into a single word, "Gravity." The research has been published in Science Advances. "Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," [said Dr. Charles Woffinden from the School of Mathematics and Physics]. "While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block." items.title: Continuations in Practice: What SE-0564 Split Continuations Changes
items.summary: Most iOS codebases still have callback APIs at their edges: an analytics SDK, a Bluetooth stack, a payment library, an old networking layer nobody wants to rewrite. Continuations are how those APIs become async functions. The conversion looks trivial, but it is the place I have seen the most subtle concurrency bugs: tasks that hang forever, crashes that only happen under load, and cancellation that silently does nothing. This article covers how continuations behave in real code, the three classic bugs (double resume, missing resume, ignored cancellation) and how to fix each one with today's APIs. It then covers what SE-0564: Split continuations changes. items.title: Two Android iOS ports with an AI agent: 24 days, then 5. The process and what broke
items.summary: The most valuable thing I got from porting my first Android app to iOS wasn't the iOS app itself. It was everything I could reuse when I started the second one. I'm an independent app developer. I have two language-learning apps on Google Play, one for Hebrew and one for Korean. Both are built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, with roughly 46,000 lines of Kotlin each. This autumn I ported both to native Swift and SwiftUI using Claude Code to write most of the code. The Hebrew app took 24 days from the first commit to the build I submitted to the App Store. The Korean app took five days of coding and 140 commits. It was live 14 days after the first commit. I have a simple principle: generate value, not lines of code. I don't particularly care how many lines an AI agent can write in an hour. I care whether the resulting app works, whether its behaviour is correct, and whether I can maintain it afterwards. What made the second port faster wasn't simply the ability to generate Swift code. items.title: The Smallest Thing on My Mac Was Eating All 16 GB of RAM
items.summary: How to check memory usage on Mac in Terminal: the 6 commands I ran, real output from a 16 GB M4, and the one that caught the leak. It was around 1 am and I was testing a Mac screen recorder I'm building. I pressed record, the countdown said "1, Get ready…", and then nothing. No timer. No Stop button. I opened Activity Monitor. My little app was using 16 GB of memory. My Mac is a MacBook Air M4 with 16 GB of RAM. So one menu bar app was asking for the whole machine. Activity Monitor is good at telling you how much. It's bad at telling you why, or whether the number is still growing. For that I went to Terminal. If you want to check memory usage on Mac in Terminal, these are the six commands I used that night, with the real output from my machine, and what each one is actually good for. A browser using 1.3 GB is normal. An app that uses 200 MB and then 300 MB and then 400 MB, every few seconds, is a leak. Most guides show you how to read memory once. SwiftUI stores the value outside the view struct itself, so it survives the view being redrawn. struct CounterView: View { @State private var count = 0 var body: some View { Button("Count: \(count)") { count += 1 } } } @State properties should almost always be marked private - the whole point is that this state is owned by this view alone. @StateObject is for when a view needs to create and own an instance of a class conforming to ObservableObject. items.summary: Longtime Slashdot reader AmiMoJo shares a report from The Guardian: For the first time, the world has experienced six consecutive days of temperatures 2C warmer than preindustrial levels, the Guardian has learned. This record hot streak, which is continuing, is too brief to signify that the upper range of the Paris climate agreement target has been breached, but scientists said it was an early indication of what is to come unless fossil fuel emissions are rapidly eliminated. It is also likely to feed into growing scientific concerns that global heating may be accelerating. The daily global surface temperature rose to its highest ever point above preindustrial levels, 2.24C, on Monday, the most recent day for which data is available, and is forecast to persist at similarly high levels for at least several more days. "This will amplify the buildup of CO2 in the atmosphere driven by fossil fuel burning," said Richard Betts, the head of climate impacts research at the Met Office Hadley Centre. items.title: FAA Identifies Patches for Last Week's Flight-Grounding Router Issue. But Was Staffing an Issue?
items.summary: CNN published an exclusive report Tuesdayon what caused last week's nationwide ground stop for flights in the U.S.. A source familiar with the Federal Aviation Administration's investigation says they've recreated the issue in a lab "and believe they found the culprit." Investigators have focused on determining why a new router at a remote Arkansas radio site overwhelmed the nation's air traffic control system with a massive amount of data, triggering gaps in radar and radio communications. They found an overlooked router setting affected how it interfaced with other decades-old routers that the FAA is decommissioning, the source said. Investigators believe software updates are needed and that those patches will prevent a repeat of the system failure... This month's ground stop not only focused attention on upgrades being made to the aging system, which have been paused as the agency investigated the incident, but also raised questions about FAA oversight of private companies charged with maintaining the network... items.title: Huawei Is Guilty of Conspiracy To Steal Trade Secrets, a US Jury Finds
items.summary: The Associated Press reports: A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiring to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of gear for wireless telecommunications networks. But jurors acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy, a result that the company's lawyer said was a "profound rejection" of the government's narrative that it was corrupt from top to bottom and had a corporate culture of cheating, stealing and lying. Prosecutors had used the charge, commonly found in organized crime and drug cases, to accuse Huawei of operating illicitly to poach intellectual property and technological secrets from competitors and partners. The convictions covered allegations that the company did business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions — including Iran and North Korea — and made false statements to U.S. government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds. items.title: What VP ≠ VNP Means (3 minute read)
items.summary: The Anthropic proof that VP≠VNP means that there is no way to find the permanent of a matrix of 0s and 1s if we are limited to arithmetic circuits of size polynomial in the input-size. This means that for P to equal NP, there must be some trick to computing permanents using AND/OR/NOT on the bits of the input that is better than addition and multiplication. There are many problems where access to Boolean operators is helpful, but it isn't clear how they would help with the permanent. There is a $1 million prize for a solution to this problem.

items.title: Recursive Self-Editing: LLMs Program Their Own Weight Edits for Self-Improvement (1 minute read)
items.summary: Today's language models improve themselves through data, training recipes, or scaffolds. Whenever their weights change, gradient descent writes the update, not the model. SELFWRITE lets the model write its own weights. Each generation, the current model studies its own reasoning on fresh training problems, inspects its own weights and activations in a persistent Python session, and writes a program that constructs a low-rank weight edit for itself from white-box primitives. It can raise gate accuracy and accuracy on a held-out test split that the loop never sees without a single gradient step.

items.title: Supercharging transformer residual connections (4 minute read)
items.summary: Google's DeepCrossAttention (DCA) enhances transformer residual connections by allowing each layer to dynamically select and route features from preceding layers, reducing information dilution and parameter count by 30-40%. Unlike traditional residual connections, DCA uses dynamic routing and depth-wise cross-attention mechanisms to achieve faster convergence and better quality with minimal parameter increase. Tested on large datasets like C4 and LM1B, DCA improves training efficiency and perplexity compared to standard models, proving a shift towards dynamic residual routing for scalable LLMs.

items.title: AI x Bio is not _just_ a data problem (14 minute read)
items.summary: How far AI gets in biology will depend largely on how much data we have. It will also depend on what is measured and the quality of that data. items.title: The most important number in AI (42 minute read)
items.summary: The Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) is a measure of AI progress developed by Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization. It is designed to be continuously updatable, and researchers can use it to look at trends going back years and forecast things for future models. This post covers how the ECI is constructed, the challenges of benchmark selection, whether it makes sense to talk about 'model IQ', whether static benchmarks stay relevant as models get better, and much more.

items.summary: d1.2 and d1.2-ultra are decision models that support audio input. They can also read a value from the input, find every passage of a kind in a text, locate things in a picture, estimate a number, and pick every option that applies. d1.2-ultra ranks first among decision models on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1. Both models are available on the Liquid API at $0.02 per million input tokens for d1.2 and $0.042 per million input tokens for d1.2-ultra.

items.title: Introducing spatial CSS: A developer preview (9 minute read)
items.summary: There has been a dramatic rise in the number of websites showing 3D content in the last few years. Spatial web standards should support designing for browsers wherever they run. Safari on visionOS 27.3 comes with a limited feature preview of the proposed spatial CSS API. This article demonstrates how to use the first components of spatial CSS through a case study.

items.title: When will humans actually fly on Starship? (3 minute read)
items.summary: Starship is now rapidly moving toward rapid reusability, but all estimates of human spaceflight on the vehicle should be taken with a gigantic grain of salt. There will be different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth. The first people to fly on Starship probably won't launch from or land on Earth, as they will probably be NASA's lunar astronauts. Humans will likely not land on Earth in Starship before 2030.
